messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In those lines, Majeed does not appear in exactly the same mode as the cunning and apathetic figure he is elsewhere in the narrative. There is a shift from indifference or cold calculation to urgent action. He commands, “Wake up, Bibi,” and declares, “I am going to take both of you to the village.” He also physically carries Jamila and covers her with a quilt. Those details soften the image of apathy. He is not leaving them exposed, frozen, or helpless. The image of him being blinded by “brilliant moonlight” also humanizes him: he is not a fully omniscient schemer here, but a hurried, vulnerable man moving through danger.

However, the same lines do not make him a purely benevolent rescuer. His speech is not tender or consensual; it is directive. He is “taking both of you,” which suggests that he is deciding for them and moving them according to his plan. Rahima being “bewildered at his heels” implies that she is not fully in control of the situation. The “thin quilt” signals practical urgency rather than deep tenderness. So, while his apathy is reduced, some of the same controlling, strategic aspect of his character remains visible. He is still leading, managing, and possibly using the journey as a way to secure a safer outcome.

Ethically, I would read the action as more teleological than deontological. A deontological reading would ask whether Majeed is saving Rahima and Jamila because it is his duty, because they matter as persons, and because the act itself expresses good-will, independent of what happens afterward. The passage gives some evidence of protection and perhaps familial responsibility, especially if they are his family. But because the broader narrative presents him as cunning and apathetic, it is difficult to treat this moment as pure good-will.

A teleological reading fits better: Majeed chooses to take them to the village because that movement is likely to produce a desirable consequence—safety, concealment, escape, survival, or avoidance of exposure. His care for Jamila, especially the act of wrapping her in the quilt, may be genuine, but it is also functional. It helps her survive the journey. The moral weight of the act lies heavily in its likely outcome: he is trying to reach a safer end.

So the scene does not erase Majeed’s earlier traits, but it complicates them. He is not simply cold or indifferent here; he is decisive, protective, and possibly calculating. He may be saving them, but not necessarily from a clean deontological good-will. The more plausible reading is that his rescue is a well-calculated, consequence-driven act: morally effective, perhaps partly compassionate, but still shaped by his pragmatic need to reach a safer outcome.

Palindromes included: level, radar, kayak, rotor, refer, reviver, madam, minim, civic, tenet, stats.
